name: Attacking the Person
short: Rejecting an argument because of who made it instead of what it says.
debate: "My opponent goes to a private school, so of course she thinks vouchers are fine." Her school doesn't make her evidence wrong; answer the evidence.
fix: Answer the argument. If a source's bias matters, say how it affects the evidence and show better evidence.

name: You Too (Tu Quoque)
short: Dismissing a criticism because the critic is guilty of the same thing.
debate: "They say our plan costs too much, but their counterplan costs money too!" Both can be expensive; the question is which cost is worth it.
fix: Compare the two costs directly instead of trading accusations.

name: Straw Man
short: Attacking a weaker or distorted version of the other side's argument.
debate: "The affirmative wants to ban all homework forever." The affirmative proposed limits on nightly homework, not a ban.
fix: Restate their argument in words they'd accept, then answer that. See Steelman vs Strawman.

name: Red Herring
short: Changing the subject to something that sounds related but isn't the point.
debate: Asked whether the carbon tax would raise gas prices, a debater talks about how important clean air is.
fix: Answer the question asked first; then explain why another issue matters more, if it does (that's weighing, not dodging).

name: Appeal to Force
short: Pressing someone to accept a claim with a threat instead of reasons.
debate: "Judges who vote for this kind of argument don't get asked back." A threat is not a reason.
fix: Give the judge a reason the argument is wrong or unfair.

name: Appeal to Pity
short: Asking for agreement because of sympathy rather than evidence.
debate: "Please vote for us; we've lost every round today." Sympathy isn't an argument on the resolution.
fix: Emotion is fair when it shows a real impact (pathos with logos). Tie the feeling to the evidence.

name: Appeal to the People
short: Claiming something is true or right because many people believe it.
debate: "Most Americans support school uniforms, so they must work." Popularity tells you what people think, not whether uniforms work.
fix: Polls can prove what voters want (sometimes relevant). Use studies to prove effects.

name: Appeals to Authority: Fair and Unfair
short: Relying on an authority outside their field, or treating one expert as the final word.
debate: "A famous actor says nuclear power is dangerous." The actor isn't an expert on reactor safety.
fix: Quote qualified experts in the field, say what their evidence is, and note where experts disagree.

name: Appeal to Ignorance
short: Claiming something is true because it hasn't been proven false (or the reverse).
debate: "No one has proven self-driving cars are unsafe, so they're safe." Lack of proof isn't proof.
fix: Say who has the burden of proof and whether they met it.

name: Begging the Question
short: Assuming the conclusion in the premises.
debate: "Zoos are wrong because keeping animals in zoos is unethical." That restates the claim.
fix: Give a reason that doesn't already assume the conclusion: a warrant.

name: Complex Question
short: A question that hides an assumption, so any direct answer accepts it.
debate: In cross-ex: "Why does your plan ignore rural students?" It assumes the plan ignores them.
fix: Answer the hidden assumption: "It doesn't; here's how it covers rural schools."

name: False Dilemma
short: Presenting two options as the only ones when there are more.
debate: "Either we fund space exploration or we feed the hungry." A budget can do some of both.
fix: Name the other options, or show why these two really are the only ones.

name: Hasty Generalization
short: Drawing a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative cases.
debate: "My cousin's school went to four days and test scores dropped, so four-day weeks hurt learning." One school is a tiny sample.
fix: Use studies of many schools, and say how large and representative the sample is.

name: False Cause
short: Assuming that because one thing followed or came with another, it caused it.
debate: "Phone use rose and so did teen anxiety, so phones caused it." The timing fits, but timing alone doesn't prove cause.
fix: Explain the mechanism and cite studies built to test cause (experiments or natural experiments).

name: Slippery Slope
short: Claiming one step will lead to a chain of extreme results without showing each link.
debate: "If we lower the voting age to 16, next it'll be 12, then 8." No link is shown.
fix: A chain argument is fair when each link has evidence. Show the links, or drop the chain.

name: Weak Analogy
short: Comparing two things that differ in ways that matter to the conclusion.
debate: "Running a country is like running a household, so the government should never borrow." Governments and households differ in key ways.
fix: Show the two cases share the features that matter, or use a closer comparison.

name: Suppressed Evidence
short: Leaving out evidence that would change the conclusion.
debate: Reading the half of a study that found benefits and skipping its finding of costs.
fix: Quote fairly. Mention important limits of your own evidence before the other side does.

name: Accident
short: Applying a general rule to a special case it wasn't meant for.
debate: "Free speech means students can say anything during a test." The general rule has reasonable limits.
fix: Ask what the rule is for, and whether this case fits that purpose.

name: Equivocation
short: Using one word in two senses in the same argument.
debate: Using "free" college to mean "no tuition" in one sentence and "costs nobody anything" in the next.
fix: Define your terms at the start and hold to the definitions.

name: Amphiboly
short: An argument that depends on a sentence that can be read two ways because of its grammar.
debate: Reading a resolution's ambiguous phrase one way in your case and the other way in rebuttal.
fix: Point out both readings and argue which one the resolution means.

name: Composition
short: Assuming the whole has a property because its parts do.
debate: "Each new rule is small, so the whole set of rules is a small burden."
fix: Look at the combined effect directly.

name: Division
short: Assuming each part has a property because the whole does.
debate: "The country is rich, so every town can afford the program."
fix: Check the parts one by one.

name: Affirming the Consequent and Denying the Antecedent
short: Two invalid ways of reasoning with if-then statements.
debate: "If the tariff worked, factory jobs would rise. Factory jobs rose, so the tariff worked." Something else could have raised them.
fix: Look for other causes, and test the claim in both directions.
